title: Word 17 — On the Gospel
attribution_note: Word 17 of 28 in the collection Short Moral-Instructive Words — see Word 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: Beloved Christians! There is nothing more pleasant, more dear, or more sweet to us sinners than the Gospel. Bread is not so welcome to the hungry, nor drink to the thirsty, nor freedom to the captive sitting in prison, as the Gospel is to sinners who have come to know their own wretchedness. *“For the Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost”* [Luke 19:10]. This is the sweetest voice of the Gospel. Who is this Son of Man? He is the Son of God, the King of Heaven and the Son of the King, sent to us by His Heavenly Father, who was willing for our sake to be called the Son of Man. Why did He come? To seek and save us who were lost, and to bring us into His eternal kingdom. What could be more welcome or more desirable to us, the lost, than this?
But let us consider what the Gospel is, what it demands of us, and to whom it is preached.
1) The Gospel, by its very name, is all-joyful news. It proclaims to the whole world Christ, the Savior of the world, *“who came to seek and to save that which was lost.”*
Listen, all you perishing sinners, listen to the sweetest voice of the Gospel! It speaks to all of us: *“The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.”*

sections.heading: Freed from Guilt, Wrath, and the Curse

pairs.en: It is dreadful for us to stand in our sins before God — but the Gospel proclaims that our sins are forgiven for the sake of Christ's name, and that Christ is our justification before God. In You, my Savior Jesus, Son of God, I shall be justified; You are my righteousness and my sanctification.

It is dreadful for us to lie under God's wrath — but the Gospel proclaims that Christ has reconciled us to God and, *“coming, preached peace to all, to those who were far off and those who were near”* [Ephesians 2:17].

The curse of the law is dreadful to us, for we are all sinners, and the law subjects the sinner to both temporal and eternal punishment. But the Gospel proclaims that Christ *“has redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us”* [Galatians 3:13].

sections.heading: Freed from Death, Hell, and Exile

pairs.en: Death is dreadful to us — but the Gospel proclaims that Christ is our resurrection and our life.
Gehenna and hell are dreadful to us — but the Gospel proclaims that Christ has delivered us from hell and from all that misery.
It is dreadful for us to be cut off from God and from His eternal kingdom — but the Gospel proclaims that *“we shall always be with the Lord”* [1 Thessalonians 4:17] in His eternal kingdom.

This, blessed Christians, is the sweetest voice of the Gospel. So then, *“taste and see that the Lord is good”* [Psalm 33:9 (34:8)]! *“For God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life.* *For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved.* *He who believes in Him is not condemned”* [John 3:16–18]. *“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, for He has visited His people and accomplished redemption for them, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David”* [Luke 1:68–69].

2) What is required of us, Christians, is that we receive with gratitude this heavenly and sweetest tidings sent down from heaven, and that we always thank from a pure heart God our Benefactor, who has shown us such mercy freely, and that out of gratitude we render Him holy obedience and pleasing service. For conscience itself urges and persuades us to be grateful to a benefactor. He has loved us, unworthy as we are — let us love Him in return, He who is worthy of all love. Love requires that we never offend the one we love. God is offended by every sin. Let us turn away from every sin, do His holy will, and not offend Him, so merciful a Father and Benefactor to us. *“Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name;* *Thy kingdom come;* *Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven”* — and so forth [see Matthew 6:10].

3) To whom is the Gospel preached? Christ Himself answers us: *“The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, for He has anointed Me to preach the gospel to the poor, and has sent Me to heal the brokenhearted”* [Luke 4:18]. That is, to those people who, coming to know their sins, see their own poverty, wretchedness, and misery, and whose hearts are broken by fear of God's judgment and by sorrow. To such as these the Gospel is preached, as a life-giving plaster is applied to a wounded body.

Listen, sorrowful and broken souls, listen to the sweetest voice of the Gospel: *“The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.”* Apply this life-giving plaster of the sweetest Gospel to your wounded souls; heal your broken hearts with this saving medicine.

*“The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost.”* He will seek and save you too, since you also are among those He came to seek and save. Do you acknowledge and confess yourselves sinners before God? Then your sins too are forgiven for the sake of Christ's name. Do you repent of your sins and carry *“godly sorrow”* [2 Corinthians 7:10]? Then salvation from God is ready for you as well. For *“this is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief”* [1 Timothy 1:15]. The Holy Spirit says to you through His servant: *“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise”* [Psalm 50:19 (51:17)]. This is the sacrifice that a repentant and broken heart offers to God, and it is more pleasing to Him than any other offering. Upon such a sacrifice God looks with mercy and sends down His grace [see Isaiah 66:2].

From this you see, Christian, that the Gospel does no good to those Christians who live fearlessly and lawlessly, who do not recognize their own sins, poverty, and wretchedness, and who have no broken heart. For what good does oil do a stone? A plaster is applied to a wound, and healing is given to one who recognizes and acknowledges his own infirmity. To such people it is said: *“Lament and mourn and weep!* *Let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to gloom.* *Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will lift you up”* [James 4:9–10]. And again: *“Even now the ax is laid to the root of the trees: every tree which does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire”* [Matthew 3:10].

Sinners! Let us fear the Dread Judgment of God, and let us strive to have a broken and humble heart, so that we too may draw from the Gospel, as from a saving spring, the living water of refreshment and comfort, and water our souls with it, and so obtain eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. To Him be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto ages of ages. Amen.
